what: RadNet operates diagnostic imaging centres. It runs hundreds of outpatient facilities in the United States where patients have MRI, CT, PET, ultrasound and mammography scans, usually in partnership with local hospital systems, and it develops artificial intelligence software to read the images.
customers: Patients referred by doctors for imaging, with payment coming from health insurers, Medicare and hospital partners; also hospital systems that run imaging jointly with RadNet.
money: Fees for scans performed at outpatient centres, paid by insurers and government programmes.
Artificial intelligence software for reading mammograms and other images, sold to other providers.
moat: Imaging centres have high fixed costs — an MRI machine and the building around it — so the operator with the most scans per machine in a local market has a cost advantage nobody else can match there. Density also matters to insurers, who want a network covering a whole region, and to referring doctors, who send patients where appointments are available.
risks: A trailing net loss of $22.4M on $2.4B of revenue, and a price/earnings ratio that cannot be calculated.
The shares trade at about 27.4 times EV/EBITDA and 47.6 times free cash flow, which is a very high price for a capital-intensive service business.
Debt of $1.9B against $767.2M of cash is heavy, and imaging equipment requires continuous replacement capital.
Reimbursement rates are set by insurers and Medicare, and imaging has historically been a target for rate reductions.
Eight analysts average a $97.00 target, about 40% above the current price, on a company currently making a loss.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $1.3B in 2021 to $2.0B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $2.4B.
Outpatient imaging is substantially cheaper than hospital imaging, so insurers actively push volume toward centres like RadNet’s.
Local market density gives genuine cost and network advantages that cannot be replicated by a new entrant.
The artificial intelligence business, particularly in mammography screening, could become a separate high-margin revenue stream.
Joint ventures with hospital systems secure referral flow that an independent operator would have to compete for.
watch: Scan volumes and revenue per scan. Imaging is a fixed-cost business, so volume determines profitability and the reimbursement rate determines whether volume is worth having.
view: Imaging is a fixed-cost business and everything about RadNet follows from that. An MRI machine and the premises around it cost the same whether they run six scans a day or sixteen. So the operator with the most volume per machine in a given market has a cost position nobody else there can match, and local density — not national scale — is the thing that matters. RadNet has built that density in specific regions and it is a genuine advantage.

The structural tailwind is real and worth stating clearly: an outpatient imaging centre is substantially cheaper than a hospital radiology department for the same scan, so insurers actively steer volume toward centres like RadNet’s. That is a durable force and it does not depend on the economy. The joint ventures with hospital systems are a clever accommodation of the same dynamic — rather than competing with hospitals for referrals, RadNet partners with them and secures the flow.

The artificial intelligence business is the part generating most of the excitement and the least of the revenue. Software that reads mammograms could in principle become a high-margin product sold to other providers, and that is a different and better business than operating scanners. But it is about 5% of revenue today, and the gap between an interesting capability and a profitable software franchise is wide and frequently not crossed.

Where I cannot follow the market is the valuation. A trailing net loss, 27.4 times EV/EBITDA, 47.6 times free cash flow and $1.9 billion of debt against a capital-intensive business that must continuously replace expensive equipment. Reimbursement rates are set by insurers and Medicare, imaging has historically been a target for rate cuts, and a leveraged fixed-cost operator has very little protection if rates fall. Eight analysts at $97 against a $69.51 price are pricing the AI story. Scan volumes and revenue per scan are the business; I would want the price to reflect that rather than the software.
bull: Insurers keep steering volume from hospitals to cheaper outpatient centres, local density compounds the cost advantage, and the AI mammography business becomes a real high-margin franchise.
bear: Reimbursement rates fall on a leveraged fixed-cost operator, equipment replacement consumes the cash flow, and the AI business never scales beyond 5% of revenue.
